title: "What a year of lending tools taught a small community library"
description: "Northbank Tool Library's first twelve months: members, loans, the tools that never came back, and what the booking system does for you."
---

# What a year of lending tools taught a small community library

Northbank Tool Library opened its roller door on 1 March 2025 in a borrowed shed behind the community hall. Twelve
months later it had 214 members and 380 tools on the shelves, almost all of them donated.

## Who borrowed what

Members took out 1,146 loans in the first year, which works out to about five loans per member. Most of those were
small jobs: a drill for a weekend, a ladder for gutters, a pressure washer before a sale.

The volunteer coordinator, Sam Okafor, put it plainly in the annual report: "We've had more drills borrowed than any
other tool, by a long way." That matched what the volunteers saw at the counter every Saturday morning.

Not everything came home. Nine tools were never returned, and the library wrote them off in February rather than
keep chasing. That's a loss rate most lenders would envy, though it still stung when one of the nine was the only
tile cutter.

## Paying for it

The library ran on a $3,200 grant from the local council in its first year, which covered public liability insurance
and the booking software. Members pay nothing to join. Donations of tools did the rest.

## What the booking system does

The library books loans through ExampleLend, an online lending platform. It sends each borrower a reminder email two
days before a loan is due. On the free plan it doesn't send text messages, so the volunteers ring anyone who is more
than a week late.

If you run something similar, I'd turn the reminder on from day one. In my view it does more for returns than any
late fee would.

## What comes next

The second year starts with a waiting list for the pressure washer and a plan to open on Wednesday evenings as well
as Saturdays. The volunteers are also asking for a second tile cutter, for obvious reasons.

None of this needed a big budget. It needed a shed, a booking system that nags people politely, and a handful of
volunteers who don't mind talking about drills.
